680.title: No compulsion, again
680.hook: no compulsion (2:256), would you compel (10:99), to you your way (109:6)
680.howItsDone: Muslims often cite 2:256, 10:99 and 109:6 as the Qur'an's teaching that faith cannot be forced; surah al-Kafirun is short and widely recited, including in the sunnah prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ahl al-kitab, and your line: people of the book. Did you ask your one question about a neighbor's faith? Today, a verse this path has met before, and two more beside it. Day six hundred eighty.

The story starts with a vow. A report in Abu Dawud says that among the Ansar of Medina, the helpers of the Prophet ﷺ, a mother whose babies kept dying would promise: if this child lives, I'll raise him among the Jews. So some of their sons had grown up Jewish. Then a Jewish tribe, the Banu Nadir, was sent out of the city, and these sons were among them. Their families said: we won't let our sons go. The report says that's when a verse came down. Four words in Arabic. You may know them by heart.

Al-Baqarah, verse two hundred fifty-six, in Pickthall's translation: "There is no compulsion in religion." La ikraha fid-din. Ikrah comes from k-r-h, the root of disliking something, so compulsion here is making someone do what they inwardly refuse. The verse goes on: the right way has become clear from the wrong. Clear enough to choose, and so it must be chosen. In the report, the sons were left to their choice. Now the two verses beside it, which the path gathers today. Surah ten, Yunus, verse ninety-nine: if your Lord had willed, everyone on earth would have believed, all together. Then the Prophet himself is asked: would you then compel people until they believe? The question answers itself. In the verse, Allah could have made everyone believe, and didn't; faith is left to be chosen. Surah eighty-eight puts it more plainly: you are only a reminder; you are not a warden over them. And then the last word of a whole surah. Al-Kafirun, one hundred nine, ends: "Unto you your religion, and unto me my religion." Not a shrug. A boundary drawn with respect, by someone sure of their own way. Over the centuries, scholars debated how far 2:256 reaches. Some classical scholars limited it, or held that later verses had abrogated it; others read it as a general rule. That debate is part of the tradition. Three verses, three angles. The truth has been made clear. Even a prophet doesn't force it. And when people choose differently, each keeps their own way.

The practice: respect one choice unlike yours. Sit, and bring to mind someone close to you who chose differently: a faith, no faith, a way of living, a decision you'd never make. Notice whatever tightens in you. Now, without agreeing, try saying inside: your way is yours. Breathe with it. If there's something you've been pushing them on, picture setting it down. You can still care. You can still hope. You don't have to compel. The bell holds the time.
No compulsion. La ikraha fid-din: the heart can't be forced, even a prophet isn't a warden, and to each their own way. Today's word.
Your line: to each their own way. Today, when you want to win someone over, say your piece once, kindly, and then let it rest. Day six hundred eighty.

681.title: War and peace, in context
681.hook: fight those who fight you and don't transgress (2:190), incline to peace (8:61), read with their occasions
681.howItsDone: Muslim scholars read verses about fighting together with their occasions of revelation (asbab an-nuzul), surrounding verses and hadith, and classical law set limits in war such as the prohibition on harming women and children.

segments.voice: Yesterday, no compulsion, and your line: to each their own way. Did you say your piece once and let it rest? Today, verses that are often quoted alone, read with their neighbors. Day six hundred eighty-one.

Take any sentence out of a novel and you can make it say almost anything. Take him, says a character, and it sounds like a kidnapping, until you read the page and find it's a chess game. Scripture can be handled the same way, by anyone, for any purpose. A handful of Qur'an verses about fighting are often clipped and passed around this way. Today, put them back on the page.

Start with the setting. For about thirteen years in Mecca, the early Muslims were persecuted and told to be patient; no fighting was permitted. After the move to Medina, surah twenty-two gives the first permission: to those who are fought against, because they have been wronged. Then al-Baqarah, verse one hundred ninety, in Pickthall's translation: "Fight in the way of Allah against those who fight against you, but begin not hostilities. Lo! Allah loveth not aggressors." The next verse, which is the one most often clipped, says to fight them wherever you meet them. But read on two verses: if they stop, Allah is forgiving, and there's to be no hostility except against wrongdoers. And in al-Anfal, verse sixty-one: "And if they incline to peace, incline thou also to it, and trust in Allah." The hadith add limits too. In al-Bukhari, the Prophet ﷺ forbade the killing of women and children in war. Muslim scholars developed a whole field for this, asbab an-nuzul, the occasions of revelation: what was happening when a verse came down, who it addressed, what came before and after. They also argued, across centuries, about how these verses fit together and what they mean for later times. The Qur'an itself doesn't settle every question in one line, and the scholars didn't pretend it did. What's clear is the method. A verse has a neighborhood. It came down into a situation. It has a sentence before it and a sentence after. Reading it alone isn't reading it.

The practice: read one verse with its context. Choose a verse or line you know well, from the Qur'an or from anywhere this year. Hold it in mind. Now ask three questions, slowly. What comes right before it? What comes right after? And when, or to whom, was it first said? If you don't know, notice that. That's not a failure; it's the start of reading. If you have a Qur'an or an app nearby, look it up after the bell. The bell holds the time.
Al-Anfal, the surah whose sixty-first verse says if they incline to peace, incline to it too, one of the neighbors a verse about fighting needs to be read beside. Today's word.
Your line: read it in context. Today, when a quotation, from any book or any person, makes you angry, find the sentence before and after it before you react. Day six hundred eighty-one.

682.title: Wealth as a trust
682.hook: wealth as a trust, with a right for the poor in it (51:19; 57:7)
682.howItsDone: Muslims pay zakat each year, commonly 2.5 percent of savings held above a minimum (nisab) for a lunar year, and give voluntary charity (sadaqah) at any time; many reckon zakat during Ramadan.

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-Anfal, and your line: read it in context. Did you find the sentence before and after something before reacting? Today, a theme about what's in your pocket. Day six hundred eighty-two.

A friend hands over a house key before a long trip. With it you can go in, water the plants, use the kitchen, even sleep there. But you'd never sell the sofa. It isn't yours, and you both know it. You're holding it for someone, and one day you'll hand it back. One verse of the Qur'an talks about money in much the same way, and it has a word for the person holding it.

Surah al-Hadid, verse seven, in Pickthall's translation, tells believers to "spend of that whereof He hath made you trustees." The Arabic word is mustakhlafin. It comes from kh-l-f, the root of khalifah, a successor, someone who stands in for another. In this picture, a person holds wealth that someone held before and someone will hold after, and the owner is Allah. Then surah fifty-one, and surah seventy, add the second half. In the wealth of the righteous, they say, there's a right, a known right, for the one who asks and the one who is deprived. Not a favor. A right. The money is held in trust, and part of it already belongs to someone else. Islamic law gives that part a shape in zakat: each year, a fixed share of savings above a set minimum goes to those in need. Beyond it there's sadaqah, given freely, any time. A hadith in Sahih Muslim pictures the person who says, my wealth, my wealth. The Prophet ﷺ said: what is yours of it is only what you ate and finished, wore and wore out, or gave away and so sent ahead. Everything else, you're leaving for others. And another hadith in Muslim's collection: charity never decreased wealth. The trust doesn't get smaller when you hand part of it on. It's how the trust gets kept.
screen: `ATE IT, WORE IT, OR SENT IT AHEAD.`

segments.voice: The practice: give from what you hold. Sit, and picture what you own as if it were on loan: your money, your phone, your time, your skills. Hold the thought: I'm looking after this. Then ask: whose known right is in it? A relative struggling, a neighbor, a charity you trust, a coworker who needs an hour of your help. Pick one. Decide the amount, or the hour, now, before the bell ends, and decide when you'll give it today. The bell holds the time.
Mustakhlafin. Trustees: in 57:7 wealth-holders stand in for Allah, the true owner, and in 51:19 the poor have a known right in what they hold. Today's word.
Your line: held in trust. Today, give the amount or the hour you chose, and think of it as returning, not losing. Day six hundred eighty-two.

683.title: Parents and family
683.hook: worship Allah, then be good to parents, repeated across the book (17:23; 31:14)
683.howItsDone: Muslims treat kindness to parents (birr al-walidayn) as a duty that comes right after worshipping Allah, and keeping family ties (silat ar-rahim) as a religious obligation; the Qur'an's own prayer for parents (17:24) is said in personal du'a.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mustakhlafin, and your line: held in trust. Did you give the amount or the hour you chose? Today, the people the book places right after Allah. Day six hundred eighty-three.

Take a highlighter to the Qur'an and mark the places where it says worship Allah alone. Then look at what sits right next to the highlight. In al-Baqarah, an-Nisa, al-An'am and al-Isra, the very next thing is the same: and be good to your parents. Not your nation, not your teacher, not even your own soul. In those verses, the command right after the oneness of God is about two people at a kitchen table.

Surah al-Isra, verse twenty-three: your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him, and kindness to parents. Then it gets specific. If one or both reach old age with you, don't say even uff to them, don't push them away, and speak to them with honor. Surah Luqman, verse fourteen, adds the reason, and it's the mother's: she carried him, weakness upon weakness, and his weaning took two years. Then: be grateful to Me and to your parents. Gratitude to Allah and gratitude to parents, in one breath. A hadith in al-Bukhari sharpens the picture. A man asks the Prophet ﷺ: who most deserves my good company? Your mother. Then who? Your mother. Then who? Your mother. Then who? Your father. And the book is honest that family can be hard. The next verse in Luqman says that if parents push you to worship other than Allah, don't obey them in that, but still keep company with them in this world, kindly. Disagreement doesn't cancel kindness. The circle widens to the rest of the family. Remember rahim, the womb, from five days ago, sharing a root with ar-Rahman? Keeping family ties is called silat ar-rahim, connecting the womb. A hadith in al-Bukhari says the rahim takes its name from ar-Rahman, and whoever keeps it connected, Allah keeps connected to them. Family, in this vocabulary, is mercy's own shape.

The practice: do a kindness for family. Sit and bring your family to mind, the one you were born into or the one you've found. Let a parent's face come, or a grandparent's, or whoever raised you. If they've died and you pray, you can ask mercy for them. If they're alive, picture them right now, wherever they are, doing something ordinary. Then choose one kindness you can do for any family member today: a call, a visit, an errand, a word of thanks, or simply not saying uff. The bell holds the time.
Rahim: the womb, sharing its root with ar-Rahman, the word underneath the command to keep family ties connected. Today's word.
Your line: parents come next. Today, do the kindness you chose before the day ends, even if it's small. Day six hundred eighty-three.

684.title: The earth
684.hook: don't spread corruption on the earth after it's set right (7:56)
684.howItsDone: Muslims may pray on any clean ground; Muslim environmental groups and teachers cite 7:56, 30:41 and hadith on planting trees and clearing the road as the basis for caring for the environment.

segments.voice: Yesterday, rahim, and your line: parents come next. Did your one kindness happen? Today, the ground under the whole family. Day six hundred eighty-four.

A hadith in al-Bukhari has the Prophet ﷺ say that the whole earth has been made a place of prayer for him, and pure. That's why a Muslim can pray in a field, an airport corner, a parking lot, a beach. Any clean patch of ground becomes a masjid for a few minutes. Now think about what that does to the plastic bag caught in the hedge, or the bottle in the gutter. If the earth is a mosque, that's litter on the prayer rug.

Surah al-A'raf, verse fifty-six, in Pickthall's translation: "Work not confusion in the earth after the fair ordering (thereof)." Pickthall's old English needs unpacking. The Arabic is la tufsidu fil-ard ba'da islahiha. Fasad is corruption, spoiling, things coming apart. Islah is setting right, putting in good order. So: don't spoil the earth after it has been set right. The picture is of something made well and handed over in good condition. The same verse goes on: call on Him in fear and hope; Allah's mercy is near to those who do good. Surah ar-Rum, verse forty-one, describes what happens when the warning is ignored: corruption has appeared on land and sea because of what people's hands have earned. Some readers today hear pollution in that verse; classical commentators read it as drought, loss and disorder following wrongdoing. Both readings hear the same link: what people do shows up in the land. And the hadith fill in the everyday side. In al-Bukhari, if a Muslim plants a tree or sows a field, and a bird, a person or an animal eats from it, it counts as charity for them. In a report in Musnad Ahmad, if the Hour comes while you're holding a seedling, plant it anyway. In Sahih Muslim, removing something harmful from the road is one of the branches of faith. Put those together and the earth isn't scenery. It's a place of prayer, a trust set in order, and a garden you're still allowed to plant.
screen: `ON LAND AND SEA, BY PEOPLE'S HANDS.`
`CLEAR THE ROAD: A BRANCH OF FAITH.`

segments.voice: The practice: pick up litter. First, sit and picture the ground you'll walk on today: your street, the path to the bus, the parking lot at work. See it plainly, including whatever's been dropped there. Choose one spot. Decide that when you pass it, you'll pick up one or two pieces of trash and put them where they belong. If you can, do it right after the bell. If you'd like, say bismillah as you bend down. The bell holds the time.
The earth. Al-ard: a place of prayer, set right and not to be spoiled, where planting a tree and clearing the road are counted as faith. Today's word.
Your line: don't spoil it. Today, leave one place cleaner than you found it: a table, a path, a corner of the park. Day six hundred eighty-four.

685.title: Oaths by time
685.hook: oaths by the dawn, the forenoon, the afternoon, the night: time as sacred
685.howItsDone: Muslims pray five times a day at prayer times named for the hours (fajr, dhuhr, 'asr, maghrib, 'isha'); surah al-'Asr is short and often recited, and a report says two companions would not part until one had recited it to the other.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the earth, and your line: don't spoil it. Did you leave one place cleaner than you found it? Yesterday was the ground under us. Today, the clock above it. Day six hundred eighty-five.

Check the clock right now. Whatever it says, the Qur'an has probably sworn by it. Early on, before the sun: by the dawn. Mid-morning, light at full strength: by the forenoon. Late afternoon, shadows long: by the declining day. After dark: by the night when it covers. Four surahs are named for those hours. The book doesn't only mention time. It takes oaths by it, the way it swore by the pen, the wind and the stars.

Here they are, in Pickthall's translation. Surah eighty-nine: "By the Dawn." Surah ninety-three: "By the morning hours." Surah one hundred three: "By the declining day." Surah ninety-two: "By the night enshrouding." Al-Fajr, ad-Duha, al-'Asr, al-Layl. An oath in Arabic sets something up as witness to what follows, and commentators say Allah swears by created things to draw attention to them. So the hours of the day are being held up as signs. Look at the shortest of them. Al-'Asr is three verses. By time, or by the declining day, surely the human is in loss, except those who believe and do good and urge one another to truth and to patience. 'Asr means late afternoon, and it can also mean time itself, an age. Commentators read it both ways. Imam ash-Shafi'i is reported to have said that if people reflected on this surah alone, it would be enough for them. Then notice what the daily prayers are called. Fajr, dawn. Dhuhr, midday. 'Asr, afternoon. Maghrib, sunset. 'Isha', nightfall. The names of the prayers are names of hours. Five times a day, the clock itself becomes the call. A hadith qudsi in al-Bukhari goes further. Allah says: the son of Adam curses time, but I am time; in My hand is the command, and I turn the night and the day. In this book, time isn't the thing standing between you and what matters. It's one of the things that matters, sworn by, and turning in Allah's hand.
screen: `AL-'ASR: TIME, AND THE HUMAN IN LOSS.`

segments.voice: The practice: notice the time of day. Without checking a clock, look around. Where is the light coming from? Is it thin, full, slanting, gone? What does the air feel like, the noise outside, your own energy? Name the hour to yourself by its look, not its number: early, full morning, the long afternoon, dusk, deep night. Then, if you'd like, say the oath of this hour once, quietly: by the dawn, by the morning hours, by the declining day, or by the night. The bell holds the time.
Al-'Asr. By the declining day, or by time itself: a three-verse surah Imam ash-Shafi'i said would be enough for people, if they reflected on it. Today's word.
Your line: by time. Today, at two different hours, stop for a few seconds and notice the light, the way you did just now. Day six hundred eighty-five.

686.title: Death as return
686.hook: death as a return, not an ending (2:156; 3:185)
686.howItsDone: Muslims say "inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un" on hearing of a death or any loss; they bury the dead quickly, pray the funeral prayer together, and visit graves, greeting the dead with peace.

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-'Asr, and your line: by time. Did you catch the light at two different hours? Time runs out for everyone, and today the book says where it runs to. Day six hundred eighty-six, the end of a week.

When a Muslim hears that someone has died, a neighbor's father, a celebrity, a friend's baby, the first words are very often the same. Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un. People say it in hospital corridors, in group chats, under their breath at the news, before they've even taken it in. And if you listen to the words, they don't mention death at all. They talk about going back home.

Al-Baqarah, verse one hundred fifty-six, describes the patient as those who, when a misfortune strikes them, say, in Pickthall's translation: "Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning." Two halves. We belong to Allah. And to Him we return. Raji'un comes from r-j-', the root of going back to where you came from. Death, in this sentence, isn't a wall. It's a road home. Al 'Imran adds the plain fact underneath: "Every soul will taste of death." No exceptions, and the verse says it without fear: the full reward comes on the Day of Resurrection. Between death and that Day, the Qur'an speaks of a barzakh, a barrier, a waiting, in surah twenty-three. What it's like, the Qur'an doesn't describe in detail; the hadith say more, and scholars discuss them carefully. A hadith in Sahih Muslim shows the words at work. Umm Salamah heard the Prophet ﷺ teach that whoever is struck by loss and says, to Allah we belong and to Him we return, and asks Allah to reward them and replace it with better, will be given better. When her husband Abu Salamah died, she said it, and thought, who could be better than Abu Salamah? Later the Prophet himself proposed to her. And graves aren't to be avoided. Another hadith in Muslim's collection says: I had forbidden you to visit graves; now visit them. A second report there gives a reason: they remind you of death. A cemetery, in this vocabulary, isn't the place where things end. It's a waiting room for a return.

The practice: visit a grave, or remember one. If you can visit a grave this week, plan when. For now, sit and bring to mind someone who has died. See their face, their hands, the sound of their voice. Don't push the grief away if it comes. Then, if you'd like, say the words softly: inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un. We belong to Allah, and to Him we return. If you pray, you can ask mercy for them. Stay with them a little longer. The bell holds the time.
Raji'un. Returning: in 2:156 the patient say we belong to Allah and to Him we are raji'un, going back to where we came from. Today's word.

Your line: a return. This week ran from no compulsion, read it in context, held in trust, parents come next and don't spoil it, to by time. Today, tell someone one good memory of a person who has died. Day six hundred eighty-six.

original.say: IN-naa lil-LAA-hi wa IN-naa i-LAY-hi raa-ji-'OON
original.note: Arabic, 2:156: we are Allah's, and to Him we are returning.

trapdoor: what you thought: inna lillahi is the Muslim way of saying rest in peace.
what it means: we belong to Allah and to Him we return: death as a road home, said at any loss.
what a scholar hears: raji'un, from r-j-', return to where you began; 23:100 names the barzakh between death and the Day.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 976 (visit graves, for they remind you of death)
